title: Flood Fill — BFS/DFS from starting cell.
shortTitle: Flood Fill — BFS or DFS spreading from a starting cell

s1_definition.profdef: Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new color, and repaints the starting cell plus every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the original color, stopping at boundaries and at cells of a different color. It is implemented with either breadth-first search using a queue or depth-first search using recursion or an explicit stack, both running in O(m times n) time and visiting each connected same-color cell once.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India plotting a map of branches where each cell is a region and the color is a risk rating. The risk team taps one region rated "medium" and says "reclassify this whole connected medium zone as high." The change spreads outward from the tapped region to every touching region that was also medium, like paint spreading across connected tiles, and it stops where the rating is different.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flood Fill spreads a new value outward from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value, using BFS or DFS, each cell touched once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new color, and repaints the starting cell plus every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the original color, stopping at boundaries and at cells of a different color. It is implemented with either breadth-first search using a queue or depth-first search using recursion or an explicit stack, both running in O(m times n) time and visiting each connected same-color cell once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India plotting a map of branches where each cell is a region and the color is a risk rating. The risk team taps one region rated "medium" and says "reclassify this whole connected medium zone as high." The change spreads outward from the tapped region to every touching region that was also medium, like paint spreading across connected tiles, and it stops where the rating is different.

**One line to remember:** Flood Fill spreads a new value outward from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value, using BFS or DFS, each cell touched once.

sections.s2_technical:
The input is a grid, a start row and column, and a replacement value. We first read the original value at the start cell. If the original value already equals the replacement, we return immediately, otherwise a naive recursion would loop forever because the repainted cells still match.

In the depth-first approach we recurse from the start cell. The base cases are going out of bounds or landing on a cell whose value is not the original value. Otherwise we set the cell to the new value and recurse into its four neighbors. Setting the value before recursing is what prevents revisiting, because neighbors will now see the new value and stop.

In the breadth-first approach we push the start cell into a queue and set it to the new value. We repeatedly pop a cell and, for each of its four neighbors that is in bounds and still holds the original value, we set that neighbor to the new value and push it. We change the value at the moment we enqueue so no cell is enqueued twice.

Both run in time proportional to the number of cells, with space proportional to the size of the connected region for the recursion stack or the queue. A senior nuance is the early return when the new value equals the old value; without it the depth-first version recurses infinitely and the breadth-first version enqueues forever. Another nuance is that marking at enqueue time, not dequeue time, is what guarantees each cell is processed exactly once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a geographic risk grid where each cell is a small zone holding a risk code. When a fraud cluster is confirmed in one zone, the risk team must escalate the entire connected block of zones that currently share the same risk code, because fraud tends to spread through adjacent connected zones.

This is exactly how Flood Fill works. From the confirmed zone the new risk code spreads to every connected zone of the same original code.

Problem 2 — If the confirmed zone already carries the escalated code, re-running the escalation must do nothing rather than spin forever.

This is exactly why we check whether the new value already equals the original value and return immediately, which keeps the operation safe to repeat.

The code will have an `Account` class for flavor, a `RiskZoneFiller` class with both a `floodFillDfs` and a `floodFillBfs` method, and a runnable demo that escalates a connected zone and prints the grid before and after.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 risk grid, start cell [0][0] holding 2, new value 3.

Step 1: The original value at [0][0] is 2, which is not equal to the new value 3, so we proceed rather than returning early.

Step 2: We repaint [0][0] to 3 and recurse. Its down neighbor [1][0] is 2, so it is repainted and recursed; its right neighbor [0][1] is 2, repainted and recursed.

Step 3: The spread continues through every connected 2: [0][2], [1][1], and [2][1], [2][2] reachable through the connected block. Cells holding 1, and the lone 3 at [2][3], act as boundaries and stop the spread.

Step 4: The cell [2][0] holding 1 is not connected through 2, so it stays 1. The result is that the connected medium block becomes high while unrelated zones keep their codes.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    Priya Sharma escalating connected medium zone from [0][0]:
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [2, 2, 2, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [2, 2, 1, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [1, 2, 2, 3]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    Grid after escalation:
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [3, 3, 3, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [3, 3, 1, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [1, 3, 3, 3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  floodFillDfs(grid, 0, 0, newValue=3)
    │ original = grid[0][0] = 2
    ├─ original == newValue? NO → proceed
    ▼
  repaint [0][0]=3
    ├─→ [1][0]=2 → repaint 3 → spread
    ├─→ [0][1]=2 → repaint 3 → spread
    │       └─→ [0][2]=2 → repaint 3
    │       └─→ [1][1]=2 → repaint 3 → [2][1]=2 → [2][2]=2
    ▼
  boundaries: cells==1 and lone 3 stop the spread
    ▼
  connected medium block becomes high; others unchanged
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new value, and it repaints the starting cell together with every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the starting cell's original value. It is the same idea as the paint-bucket tool in an image editor, and I can implement it either with depth-first search using recursion or with breadth-first search using a queue, both of which run in time proportional to the number of cells.

In the depth-first version I read the original value at the start, then recurse, and at each cell my base cases are going out of bounds or landing on a cell whose value is not the original value. Otherwise I set the cell to the new value before recursing into its four neighbors, and setting the value first is exactly what stops me from revisiting, because the neighbors now see the new value and stop. In the breadth-first version I enqueue the start, and for each dequeued cell I enqueue every in-bounds neighbor that still holds the original value, marking it at the moment I enqueue so no cell is ever enqueued twice.

The single most important guard is the early return when the new value already equals the original value. Without that check the depth-first version recurses forever and the breadth-first version enqueues forever, because repainted cells still appear to match. Marking cells at enqueue time rather than dequeue time is the other detail that guarantees each cell is processed exactly once.

In my project at National Bank of India, we maintained a geographic risk grid where each cell was a zone carrying a risk code, and when a fraud cluster was confirmed in one zone we needed to escalate the entire connected block of zones sharing that code, because fraud tends to spread through adjacent connected areas. Flood Fill did exactly that, and the early-return guard made the escalation safe to re-run without ever looping, which mattered because the risk team sometimes triggered the same escalation twice.
